Validation outputs · 2026-09-17

What the cut-point model is asked to do, and how it fails

The evaluation task, in one paragraph

Each test case is one robot-head photo of a tomato plant (848×408 px, plus the matching depth map for RGB-D models) and one query pixel that lies on the target leaf stalk (petiole), away from the stem. The model must trace that stalk to where it joins the main stem and return the cut point: 10 mm along the stalk from the junction, as image coordinates (and depth). If the junction area is hidden behind a leaf, fruit or stem, the correct answer is to abstain (return no point). A point counts as a hit if it lies within 2 px of the 10–20 mm admissible interval; at this camera distance 10 mm is about 8.5 px and the stalks are 4–5 px wide. The 1,358 test cases come from 4 plants the model never saw in training: 1,012 with a visible cut, 346 with an occluded one.

query pixel (given)label cut point10–20 mm intervalmodel prediction — tiles are zoomed crops; "query outside crop" means the given pixel lies beyond the zoom window.

A Visible, correctanswer within 5 px (~6 mm) of the label5%13%

C Visible, wrong structurepoint on another petiole, stem, or the background, >25 px away25%24%
D Visible, wrongly abstainedcut was visible but the model said occluded29%3%
E Occluded, correct abstentioncut region hidden; model correctly returned null48%54%
F Occluded, fabricated pointcut region hidden; model still returned a point52%46%

A–D are shares of the 1,012 visible cases; E–F of the 346 occluded cases. The untrained model gives an invalid answer on 100% of cases (below).

The issues, in order of severity

  • Fabricated points on hidden cuts (F). The best model still returns a point for 46% of occluded targets. For a robot this is the dangerous error: a confident coordinate for something the camera cannot see. Thresholding the model's own point-vs-null confidence at the class base rate lowers it to 32%; a native-depth consistency check lowers it further, at a cost in coverage.
  • Near misses dominate (B). 60% of visible answers land on the right stalk but 5–25 px (6–30 mm) from the label. Only 12.5% are within 5 px and 5% inside the 10–20 mm interval. The stalk is 4–5 px wide and each image token covers 32×32 px, so this sits at the resolution limit of the input.
  • Wrong structure (C). 24% of visible answers land on a different stalk, the stem, or the background more than 25 px away. The RGB model's misses were mostly on the background ~1.4 m behind the plant; the depth-aware model reduced but did not remove this.
  • Data ceiling. 11,520 training rows cover only 168 targets; 10 of 39 test targets are occluded in every view, and the occlusion rate varies 1–43% by plant, so the label can be predicted from identity. This is why RGB models never learned occlusion as a visual cue (AUC 0.58–0.64) and why re-collection is the main lever.

Untrained model: all 1,358 outputs are the identical string above. It abstains on everything and pairs that with inspect_cut_region, which the contract forbids for an abstention, so every answer is invalid; it cannot do the task in either direction. RGB fine-tune: valid JSON everywhere; localizes the visible cases but 21–34 px off here, and returns a point for the second occluded frame. Depth-aware fine-tune: 3.9 px on the first frame, the same 23 px near miss on the second, abstains correctly on the third, still fabricates on the fourth (the fruit-occluded case). The frames were taken from the category sheet above, not chosen for flattering results.
